message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal pulls together several independent sources of evidence. Our access-control data show clearly that the clubs have spare daytime capacity, so new members cost us almost nothing to accommodate. A survey of 640 local non-members tells us there is real demand at £29, with identifiable target groups, and our competitors' pricing confirms that £29 sits in the market range. We have also thought about retention, not just acquisition. Our own data show members who attend classes churn at less than half the rate of those who do not, so the extra daytime classes are not a cost so much as an investment in keeping the new members we recruit. The projection is conservative at 300 new members per club, well within what the survey implies, and after fully costing the extra classes it still delivers around £193,000 a year in net revenue. Members who want more can upgrade at any time. I am confident this is a well-targeted, low-risk way to grow the business.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Introducing an Off-Peak Membership
Pulse Fitness, Commercial Team, August 2026

1. Proposal
We propose introducing an off-peak membership at £29 a month from 1 October 2026, alongside our existing standard membership at £42 a month. Off-peak members would have access before 4 pm on weekdays and all day at weekends, with full access to the gym floor and to classes running in those hours.

2. Background
Pulse operates four clubs with 9,600 standard members. Membership has been flat for 18 months, while two budget gyms have opened within our catchments, both offering memberships at £22 to £25 a month. Our clubs are busy between 5 pm and 8 pm on weekdays, when the gym floor often runs at or near capacity, but quiet during weekday daytimes, when typical utilisation is around 30%.

Access-control data for May to July 2026 show that 31% of our current standard members visit exclusively in what would be the off-peak window, and a further 22% visit mostly off-peak.

3. Market evidence
A survey of 640 non-members living within two miles of our clubs, conducted in June, found that 19% would "definitely" or "probably" join at £29 a month for off-peak access. The most interested groups were retirees, shift workers, parents of school-age children and students.

Four of our six closest competitors already offer an off-peak or daytime membership, priced between £25 and £32.

4. Classes and retention
Retention is the other half of our commercial challenge. Monthly churn among members who attend at least one class a week is 2.1%, against 4.8% among members who do not attend classes. Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week to support the new membership, which should lower churn among off-peak members towards the 2.1% level. The additional classes would cost £18,700 a month across the four clubs in instructor fees.

5. Revenue projection
We expect to recruit 1,200 new off-peak members in the first year, about 300 per club, which is consistent with the survey response and the size of our catchments. At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue. After the cost of the additional classes (£224,400 a year), net additional revenue is £193,200 a year.

Because daytime utilisation is low, the additional members can be accommodated without investment in equipment or space.

6. Operational changes
Access control will be updated so that off-peak members' cards do not open the turnstiles outside their access window. Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm, giving those finishing early shifts or school pick-ups time to train. Members will be able to upgrade to standard membership at any time, and to switch between membership types with one month's notice.

7. Risks
Some standard members may perceive the off-peak price as unfair. We will communicate the change as an extension of choice. Competitor responses are possible; the budget gyms already price below our proposed off-peak rate, so we do not expect a price war.

8. Staff consultation
Club managers and front-of-house teams at all four clubs were consulted in July. Managers supported the proposal, noting that daytime classes are often under-filled and that a daytime membership would help build a regular community at quieter times. Front-of-house staff asked for clear signage and app messaging about access hours, which we will provide before launch.

9. Recommendation
The off-peak membership fills spare daytime capacity, responds to competitor offers and targets clearly identified customer groups. We project net additional revenue of around £193,000 a year and recommend launch on 1 October 2026.
</document>
response:
# Review: Off-Peak Membership Proposal

**Overall:** The arithmetic is correct (£417,600 − £224,400 = £193,200), but the £193k headline isn't reliable. The biggest omission is that the proposal doesn't model the cost of its own supporting data, and the retention argument rests on a causal claim the evidence can't support.

## Major issues

**1. Cannibalisation is missing from the projection and the risk section.**
The access data in section 2 show 31% of current standard members (about 2,976) visit only in the off-peak window, and another 22% (about 2,100) visit mostly off-peak. Section 6 lets members switch types on one month's notice. Each member who downgrades from £42 to £29 costs £156 a year.
- Break-even against the £193k is roughly 1,240 downgraders, about 13% of all members or 42% of exclusive off-peak users.
- If half of the exclusive off-peak members switch, the net result is about −£39k.
- The proposal presents this data as evidence of spare capacity, but it is equally evidence of how much existing revenue is exposed.

**2. The retention argument confuses correlation with causation.**
Members who attend classes churn less (2.1% vs 4.8%), but engaged members are more likely to both attend classes and stay. Nothing shows that adding classes lowers churn, especially among a new, differently motivated segment. "Classes clearly keep members loyal" is an assumption.

**3. The classes are a pure cost in the numbers.**
The projection includes no retention benefit, so the £224k appears only as a deduction. Calling it "an investment" is not backed by anything in the model. Section 8 also says managers report daytime classes are often under-filled, which suggests off-peak members could use existing classes. The case for six extra classes per club is not made.

**4. The 1,200-member figure is treated as a full-year average.**
Revenue of £417,600 assumes 1,200 members paying for all 12 months. In reality:
- Members arrive over the year. With a linear ramp, average paying members would be about 600, giving roughly £209k revenue against £224k of class costs, so the net is about zero or slightly negative.
- Churn of 2–5% a month (the proposal's own figures) erodes the base further.

**5. "Conservative" and "consistent with the survey" aren't demonstrated.**
- 19% is stated intent ("definitely or probably"). Stated intent typically overstates real uptake, and the proposal applies no discount.
- No calculation links 19% of 640 to 300 per club (catchment population, share reached, conversion).
- Only £29 was tested, so the survey says nothing about price sensitivity.
- The survey method and sampling aren't described.

## Smaller issues

- **Inconsistent access window:** Section 1 says before 4 pm, section 6 says until 5 pm. The 4–5 pm gap matters for cannibalisation and for the early-evening peak.
- **Competitor logic:** Four of six rivals charging £25–32 shows £29 is plausible, not that Pulse will win share. The budget gyms at £22–25 undercut the offer, and "they're already cheaper, so no price war" is weak reasoning.
- **Seasonality:** Utilisation data are from May–July, and the survey was in June. Autumn and winter patterns may differ.
- **Capacity claim vs. cost:** "New members cost almost nothing" sits oddly with £224k of added class cost, which is over half the new revenue. Marketing, staffing, and signage costs also aren't included.
- **Upgrade revenue:** "Can upgrade at any time" is offered as upside but isn't quantified, and upgrades are likely outweighed by downgrades.
- **Timeline:** The recommended launch date of 1 October 2026 has passed, so the plan needs updating, or actual results should replace the projection.

## What I'd ask for before approval

1. A downgrade scenario (e.g. 5%, 15%, 30% of off-peak-heavy members), or a design change that limits it, such as a lock-in period, no downgrades in the first 6–12 months, or a narrower window.
2. A monthly ramp with churn applied, giving a realistic year-one figure.
3. Evidence for the classes' effect, such as a pilot at one club, or at least the churn comparison controlled for tenure and visit frequency. Otherwise, test the offer with existing classes first.
4. A derivation of 300 per club, with a discount applied to the stated-intent figure.
5. A reconciled access window.

The idea may still be sound, since filling a 30%-utilised daytime period is a reasonable goal. But as written, the downside is understated, and "low-risk" and "conservative" are not supported.
